Feds Hit Bank of America With $1.2B Fine
|                          By Newser Editors and Wire Services                                                                                                            Posted Oct 13, 2026  5:40 PM CDT                                                       | 
The US Treasury Department said Tuesday that it's imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The fines on America's second-biggest bank amount to the third-largest in the department's history, the AP reports. Regulators said the bank failed for years to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, reports CNBC.
- "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."
- Treasury said Bank of America also reached an $11.6 million settlement with the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."
In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.'' The penalty includes $750 million that will go to the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency. Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated'' the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering.
- The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4 billion settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3 billion settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year. Both those historic actions happened as part of the Biden administration's focus on anti-money laundering and efforts to promote compliance with the then-emerging virtual currency industry.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,'' Bank of America said in a statement. "We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators." Bank of America, which is due to report quarterly earnings Wednesday morning, fell more than 2% in after-hours trading after the fine was announced.

Bank of America Hit With $1.2 Billion Fine Over Failure to Report $5 Billion in Suspicious Transactions
Regulators said the bank delayed reports on over $5 billion in suspicious transactions and breached sanctions rules
Bank of America faces more than $1.21 billion (£907.5 million) in US regulatory penalties and settlements after authorities found widespread failures in its anti-money laundering controls and delayed reporting of suspicious financial activity.
The enforcement actions, announced on 13 October 2026, concern failures to report more than $5 billion (£3.75 billion) in suspicious transactions promptly, alongside apparent violations of US sanctions programmes.
National Security Risks and Compliance Failures
The US Treasury Department said more than $1 billion (£750 million) of that activity involved national security-related and other priority risks. These included transactions potentially linked to Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and trade-based money laundering connected to the US south-western border.
Bank of America admitted to wilful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. The findings concern failures in the bank's compliance systems; they do not establish that every transaction identified as suspicious involved criminal conduct.
Why Bank of America Faces the Penalties
The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion (£900 million) penalty over the bank's failure to meet key anti-money laundering obligations.
Regulators found that the bank failed to maintain an adequate compliance programme, conduct required checks on correspondent accounts held for foreign financial institutions and file suspicious activity reports promptly.
These reports give authorities information about transactions that may warrant investigation. Delays can reduce their usefulness by allowing potentially illicit activity to continue before investigators receive the relevant information.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) separately assessed a $750 million (£562.5 million) civil penalty, the largest in its history. However, that amount is credited towards FinCEN's assessment rather than added to it.
The distinction prevents double-counting: the combined penalties do not include the OCC assessment as an additional payment on top of the full FinCEN amount.
Separately, the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an $11.6 million (£8.7 million) settlement over 475 apparent sanctions violations. Together, the FinCEN penalty and OFAC settlement amount to $1.2116 billion (£908.7 million).
What the Suspicious Transactions Figure Means
The more than $5 billion (£3.75 billion) figure represents suspicious financial activity that authorities said Bank of America failed to report promptly. It is not a finding that the entire amount was laundered or otherwise criminal.
Treasury officials identified activity indicative of Chinese money laundering networks, suspected fraud and possible trade-based money laundering with a substantial connection to the south-western border.
The separate OFAC settlement concerned apparent violations of sanctions programmes involving Iran, Russia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism, among others.
OFAC classified the apparent violations as non-egregious and said they were largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement concerns potential civil liability, distinct from the failures addressed by FinCEN and the OCC.
Earlier Regulatory Action and Required Reviews
The enforcement action follows a December 2024 OCC cease-and-desist order requiring Bank of America to address deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money laundering compliance programme.
The latest OCC penalty addresses violations of the same legal framework. FinCEN is also requiring remedial action as part of its resolution with the bank.
Bank of America must work with an independent third party to review previously undetected suspicious transactions. Additional assessments will examine its anti-money laundering controls, including transaction monitoring and checks on customers and foreign correspondent accounts.
Those reviews are intended to identify activity that should have been reported and assess whether the bank's systems can prevent similar failures.
How Bank of America Responded
Bank of America said it had invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combating financial crime. It also said work on the corrective measures required by regulators was well advanced.
The bank said its third-quarter results would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion (£900 million), reducing net income by approximately 17 US cents (12.75p) per share. The enforcement action did not impose a cap on the bank's asset size.
The financial penalty therefore comes alongside continuing compliance obligations. Paying the assessment does not replace the requirement to review past activity and improve the systems used to identify and report potentially illicit transactions.

Bank of America fined $1.21 billion as regulators cite failures involving $5 billion in suspicious activity: What went wrong?
Bank of America faces a $1.21 billion US fine over failures to report suspicious transactions, with the penalty expected to hurt quarterly earnings.
Bank of America has been fined $1.21 billion by US regulators over failures to detect and report suspicious financial activity, including transactions worth more than $5 billion, as per Reuters.
According to the report, the US Treasury Department said more than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security concerns and other high-priority risks. The penalty is among the largest in the department’s history and is expected to affect the bank’s third-quarter earnings.
Bank of America failed to flag billions in suspicious activity
The US Treasury said the bank relied too heavily on information from law enforcement agencies and other financial institutions instead of using its own systems to identify potentially suspicious transactions.
Regulators also said the bank prioritised revenue while developing its compliance programmes. Its transaction monitoring systems failed to flag suspicious activity in time, delaying reports to the government.
Under a consent order, Bank of America must appoint an independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that went undetected and report it to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).
Reuters reported that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the regulator’s history. The action was linked to shortcomings identified in a 2024 cease-and-desist order.

sources.news_title: BofA fined $1.21B for failures it agreed to fix in 2024
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – Federal regulators fined Bank of America $1.21 billion Tuesday after finding it failed to quickly report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and relied on others to catch what its own systems missed.
The $1.2 billion assessed by Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network includes a $750 million penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest in the agency’s history, the OCC said. The penalty will be paid to the U.S. Treasury. The Office of Foreign Assets Control separately settled 475 apparent sanctions violations with the bank for $11.6 million.
Treasury didn’t immediately respond to questions from The Center Square on Tuesday afternoon.
OCC examiners reviewing a small sample of accounts in the bank’s $102 billion credit card portfolio found 10 showing signs of potential trade-based money laundering. At the agency’s request, Bank of America reviewed those accounts and filed suspicious activity reports covering hundreds of millions of dollars in transactions in five of them. Absent the OCC’s request, the order states, “there is no indication that the Bank would have reviewed these accounts or filed these SARs.”
Between 2019 and 2023, bank management including the then-Bank Secrecy Act officer received written reports showing Bank of America was failing to file suspicious activity reports on 18% to 44% of potentially suspicious activity that was never referred for investigation, depending on the year. By 2024, the backlog of cases awaiting investigator review peaked at nearly 200,000.
The Bank Secrecy Act requires banks to file suspicious activity reports when they know or suspect a transaction involves criminal activity. Those reports go to FinCEN and feed federal investigations into drug trafficking, sanctions evasion and terrorist financing.
Treasury said the bank allowed suspicious activity to accumulate uninvestigated for extended periods, “resulting in late reporting of limited utility to law enforcement.”
More than $1 billion of the unreported activity involved national security and other priority risks, Treasury said, including transactions indicative of Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering with what the department called “a substantial nexus to the southwest border.”
Bank of America signed a cease-and-desist order with the OCC in December 2024 committing to fix the same compliance problems. The agency found Tuesday that the bank had not done so.
“Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank’s BSA/AML (anti-money laundering) compliance program continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens U.S. national and economic security,” Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould said. “The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable.”
Brian Moynihan, Bank of America’s chair and chief executive, signed the 2024 order committing to fix the deficiencies. He signed Tuesday’s penalty order as well.
“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” a Bank of America spokesperson said in an emailed statement to The Center Square. The bank said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and assigned thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and that it is “far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.” It said it supports law enforcement across thousands of investigations and files hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.
Bank of America said the penalties will result in a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share. The bank said remediation costs are already in its current expense base.
The FinCEN order requires Bank of America to hire a third party to go back through its records and identify suspicious transactions it never reported. The bank must also submit to independent reviews of its transaction monitoring, customer due diligence and foreign correspondent account programs, and of the data governance behind them.
Treasury said those reviews will evaluate the bank’s handling of three priority risks: the southwest border, cartels and potential narcotics trafficking; Iran; and Russia.
The OCC also found that Bank of America sent outgoing wire transfers with inaccurate sender information, which the order said potentially harmed law enforcement’s ability to know who sent the money.
Between November 2021 and October 2024, the bank processed roughly 33,300 such wires totaling about $1 billion. The bank identified the problem itself in April 2024 and stopped the practice that year, but does not know how long it had been going on.

Bank of America fined $1.2 billion by Treasury Department for money laundering and sanctions laws violations
By Samantha Delouya, CNN
(CNN) — The US Treasury Department on Tuesday announced it was imposing a more than $1.2 billion fine on Bank of America, accusing the bank of violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The bank, which is the second-largest in the US, failed to mitigate and report “priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in its announcement.
“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement.
“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institution[s] are not above the law,” Bessent added.
In a statement, Bank of America said it was working with regulators to reach penalty resolutions.
“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators,” a Bank of America spokesperson said. “We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.”
The spokesperson also said the Treasury Department’s penalty will impact the company’s quarterly earnings results, which are expected to be released Wednesday.
“Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share. We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base,” the spokesperson said.
The $1.2 billion fine is the third-largest ever imposed by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), following a record $3.4 billion fine against Binance in 2023 and a $1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank in 2024. Both of those fines were also accompanied by charges from the Justice Department, though there is no accompanying Justice Department action for the Bank of America fine.
The second Trump administration has taken actions against big banks for the practice of “debanking,” including through executive orders. Earlier this year, President Donald Trump also filed a $5 billion personal lawsuit against JPMorgan Chase, alleging that the country’s biggest bank closed his account for political reasons. However, the fine against Bank of America is the largest anti-money-laundering penalty the Trump administration’s Treasury Department has imposed on a major bank.
As part of the total fine, $750 million will go to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) as a civil penalty, making it the largest OCC penalty in history.
As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it willfully failed to have proper safeguards in place and failed to report suspicious activity, the Treasury Department said.
Bank of America failed to respond in a timely and meaningful way to red flags involving suspicious customers, including those with ties to narcotics trafficking, even after compliance personnel escalated concerns, Treasury said. Bank Of America Fined $1.2 Billion For Failing To Report $5 Billion In Suspicious Transactions, Including Chinese Money-Laundering Networks
Most banks spend the night before their earnings call polishing the NII slide and fudging the reserve release calculations. Bank of America will be spending it reading a Treasury press release about itself.
Just after the close on Tuesday, Treasury announced more than $1.21 billion in penalties against BofA for violating anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws. Treasury calls it the third-largest penalty in its history, and the OCC calls its piece the largest it has ever handed out. The bank admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act. It did not report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions on time, and more than $1 billion of that was tied to what Treasury calls "priority" national-security risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.
Here is how the money breaks down, per Treasury's press release:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty for the Bank's failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.
The OCC assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for the Bank's deficient and ineffective BSA/AML (anti-money laundering) compliance program.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an $11.6 million settlement agreement with the Bank over apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
The penalties don't simply add up. Per CNBC, the OCC's $750 million is credited toward FinCEN's $1.2 billion, which gets you to about $1.21 billion once OFAC's change is added. In other words, it is a $1.2 billion fine with a record attached.
"Prioritized Its Revenues"
The details are where it gets awkward. Treasury did not say BofA was simply overwhelmed. It said this:
As these issues arose, Bank of America prioritized its revenues and minimized the impact on its required compliance resources. The nature and extent of the Bank's resulting reliance on law enforcement inquiries, requests by other financial institutions, and similar interventions over its own internal, automated controls... meant that the Bank effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations.
Translation: BofA's money-laundering detection system often amounted to waiting for a subpoena.
Treasury also says the bank "allowed suspicious activity to accumulate uninvestigated for extended periods." That meant SARs arrived too late to help law enforcement much. Its customer due diligence also "failed to account for customers' extensive reliance on payments from unknown third parties," and the bank didn't act on red flags that included "potential ties to narcotics trafficking proceeds," even after its own compliance staff raised concerns about trade-based money laundering and fraud.
The OCC's language was harsher. Its release says the bank's transaction monitoring "resulted in the Bank failing to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions," that "the Bank knew for years" it was failing to escalate potentially suspicious activity, and that its BSA Officer and staff "lacked sufficient skills and expertise." Comptroller Jonathan Gould said:
"The second largest bank's egregious and continued BSA violations warrant the OCC imposing its largest [civil money penalty] ever assessed against a bank."
— Comptroller Jonathan Gould (@USComptroller) October 13, 2026
OFAC, for its part, found 475 apparent sanctions violations. They included payments routed through blocked banks and designated individuals who were allowed to withdraw funds "due to poor sanctions alert calibration." OFAC called the violations "non-egregious," which is the regulatory version of "could have been worse."
About That 2024 Order
None of this came out of nowhere. On December 23, 2024, the OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against BofA for BSA and sanctions deficiencies, "including a failure to timely file suspicious activity reports and failure to correct a previously identified deficiency related to its Customer Due Diligence processes." The order itself described a "systemic failure" to set proper transaction-monitoring thresholds. That order came with no fine, a point American Banker noted at the time. As we reported back in October 2024 (Oct 30, 2024), barely two weeks after TD's guilty plea, BofA disclosed in a filing that it was in talks with several federal regulators over its
Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance programs... including transaction monitoring, training, governance, and customer due diligence... resolution of these discussions may include one or more public orders by the regulators.
At the time we wondered which of the big US banks would be "named next" after TD. It took two years and an extra cease-and-desist, but we can now cross that question off the list.
(The same filing also disclosed a separate CFPB inquiry into payments on the Zelle network, which BofA said it might fight in court. Nothing in today's Treasury, OCC or OFAC releases mentions Zelle. That was a different matter with a different regulator.)
This time there is a fine, and the reason is what happened afterward. Per Treasury:
After agreeing to the 2024 Order, the Bank still failed to prioritize BSA/AML compliance... For example, more than a year after the 2024 Order, the Bank still failed to escalate potentially suspicious activities to investigators for review.
Put differently, the first notice was free. The follow-up came with a bill.
The TD Comparison
The obvious benchmark is TD Bank. In October 2024 TD pleaded guilty to BSA and money-laundering conspiracy charges and agreed to roughly $3 billion in total penalties across agencies, according to the DOJ. That included a $1.8 billion criminal resolution, a $450 million OCC penalty, and an asset cap on its US operations. We flagged back in May 2024 that the AML mess risked sending TD into a "lost decade."
BofA's settlement differs in a few important ways:
- About 40% of TD's total: $1.2 billion versus about $3 billion.
- Admission, not a plea: BofA admitted willful BSA violations to FinCEN. No source we've seen mentions criminal charges or a DOJ resolution.
- No asset cap: Instead of a growth restriction, BofA gets a third-party lookback and independent reviews of its monitoring, CDD and correspondent-banking due diligence. Those reviews focus on the southwest border and cartels, Iran and Russia.
- OCC records: BofA's $750 million beats TD's $450 million OCC penalty by a wide margin.
In other words, a record fine, but nothing like TD's sentence.
Some Napkin Math
BofA told CNBC the penalties mean a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge in Q3 results (perfect timing for tomorrow's Adjusted EPS to miss net of "one time almost criminal items", cutting net income by about 17 cents per share. Against the roughly $1.11 consensus EPS, that is about 15% of the quarter's expected earnings gone before the call starts.
Another way to measure it: $1.2 billion against "over $5 billion" in suspicious transactions not reported on time works out to about 24 cents per unreported dollar. As compliance budgets go, the cheaper option was always going to be the compliance budget.
The bank says remediation costs are "already reflected in its current expense base," so the hit should be one-time, at least on paper.
The Stock
The timing was unusual. BAC closed Tuesday at $53.94, down 1.2% in concert with a broader bank selloff (after what were good, if not great earnings by JPM, Citi and Goldman) but the news came out around 4:09pm ET, right after the bell. In other words, regular-session weakness came alongside a soft tape for financials and can't be pinned on the fine, and sure enough BofA sold off another 2% after hours once the news hit. That leaves BAC down about 3.6% YTD, and well below its 52-week high of $65.22.
TL/DR: the $1.2 billion is not the story. BofA can cover it with about a week of NII (6 days when the 10Y hits 6%); the story is that Treasury, the OCC and Bessent all used the same phrase about the second-largest US bank: it "prioritized its revenues" over compliance. And BofA kept doing so for more than a year after signing a cease-and-desist. For a CEO who has built his tenure on "responsible growth," that phrase will be hard to escape. The independent reviews and lookback will likely produce more late SARs, and possibly more findings, over the coming quarters.
Next catalysts:
- Q3 results, Wednesday before the open; call at 8:30am ET. Consensus is about $1.11 EPS on about $30.6–30.7 billion revenue, with FTE NII of about $16.55 billion (Zacks). BofA guided 2026 NII growth to the upper end of 6–8% in July. A Q3 NII print of $16.3 billion or more keeps that credible, per one preview.
- On the call, listen for whether management reports results excluding the 17-cent charge (it will). Also listen for any change to remediation spending or the expense outlook, whether more regulatory or DOJ exposure remains (a "no comment" will say a lot), whether buybacks are affected, and NII guidance after the September Fed move.
- Moynihan on CNBC at 10:20am ET, where "responsible growth" is likely to come up more than he'd like.
Going into the quarter, Goldman's desk said it wanted BofA to show "any NII upside updated for the rate curve and can this flow into operating leverage?" Operating leverage is easier to show without a $1.2 billion penalty line item.
Still, the main lesson for anyone thinking of skimping on AML: it costs about 24 cents on the dollar to make your (allegedly criminal) clients extra happy, and the bill eventually arrives.

US fines Bank of America $1.2B, saying it violated money laundering & sanctions law
WASHINGTON (TNND) — The U.S. Treasury Department said it is imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the penalties on Tuesday, describing them as the department's third-largest enforcement action against a financial institution. The action includes an $11.6 million settlement with the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control over apparent violations of sanctions programs involving Iran, Russia, narcotics trafficking, and global terrorism.
The penalty also includes $750 million that will go to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency.
Bessent said the penalties reflect alleged shortcomings in Bank of America's obligations to identify suspicious activity and comply with restrictions designed to prevent illicit money from flowing through the U.S. financial system.
“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," he added.
Anti-money laundering rules require financial institutions to maintain safeguards that can identify and report transactions potentially tied to crimes such as fraud, drug trafficking and terrorism financing. U.S. sanctions rules restrict dealings involving targeted countries, organizations and individuals.
The enforcement action comes as federal regulators continue to scrutinize major banks' compliance systems. Treasury has imposed multibillion-dollar penalties against financial institutions in previous cases involving alleged failures to detect or prevent illicit financial activity.

sources.news_title: BofA gets $1.21B penalty for money laundering
sources.text:
- Key insight: The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations.
- Supporting data: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's fine follows a December 2024 cease-and-desist order, over a year after which regulators found the bank had failed to address holes in compliance.
The Department of the Treasury on Tuesday announced a $1.21 billion penalty against Bank of America for willful anti-money laundering and sanctions violations, including failing to report over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions, $1 billion of which reportedly had national security implications.
In addition to the $1.2 billion fine from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a $750 million civil money penalty. The Bank also reached a $11.6 million settlement with the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control.
"Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our economic and national security," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks. Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."
According to a Treasury release, between September 2021 and April 2025, Bank of America committed over 475 U.S. sanctions violations, including processing over $14.3 million in payments through 35 "blocked banks" on the U.S.'s sanctions blacklist, involving sanctions against a number of countries, including Russia, Iran, Burma and Somalia, as well as known drug traffickers and terrorist organizations. In its release, OFAC said Bank of America acted "recklessly" and had previously received multiple cautionary letters regarding "substantially similar conduct."
According to the Treasury, the bank was aware in March 2022 that its payment directory included sanctioned banks, but that due to a combination of outdated screening filters, human error and technological failings, payments continued to these entities. The bank did conduct a review, but did not identify the full scope of the transactions until after OFAC subpoenaed the firm in January 2025.
The $750 million penalty imposed by the OCC follows up on an existing enforcement action.  The bank was already subject to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring it to address deficiencies in its anti-money laundering program, but regulators found that a year after the 2024 action, the firm still had not taken key steps to remediate the shortcomings. 
"More than a year after the 2024 Order, the Bank still failed to escalate potentially suspicious activities to investigators for review," the Treasury release noted. "Bank management failed to ensure the Bank had an effective BSA/AML compliance program and continued to minimize the program's significant deficiencies."
As part of the settlement, the bank must conduct a third-party lookback to find previously undetected suspicious transactions, as well as submit to independent reviews of its anti-money laundering governance, with particular attention to risks related to sanctioned jurisdictions.

Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the enforcement actions.
The action comes less than a week after regulators issued large settlements against another major bank. The Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, in separate, coordinated cease-and-desist actions fined American Express' banking arm $350 million on Thursday for insufficient anti-money-laundering controls, while the Federal Reserve ordered Amex's parent companies to address financial-crime deficiencies across the enterprise. The OCC, which fined Amex $350 million as part of its enforcement action, said they identified roughly $13 billion in illicit activity at the firm, including transactions with ties to bank "insiders."
The settlements mark the largest Treasury fine ever imposed on a bank and the third largest in OCC history.

Listen: the breakdown
Market briefing: The US Treasury fined Bank of America $1.2 billion for missing over $5 billion in suspicious transactions. Crypto barely noticed. BTC held near $83,117 as the headline landed with almost no market reaction.
- Bank of America fined $1.2 billion for anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures.
- The Treasury says the bank missed flagging over $5 billion in suspicious transactions.
- Crypto shrugged: BTC held near $83,117 and ETH slipped under 1% on the day.
Source: U.S. Department of the Treasury
A $1.2 billion Bank of America fine lands over $5 billion in missed transactions, yet crypto barely twitched. Does a legacy-bank penalty really move Bitcoin at all?
The US government just fined Bank of America $1.2 billion. The reason is blunt: the bank failed to flag over $5 billion in suspicious transactions.
The Treasury did not reach for soft language either. It called the bank's money-laundering and sanctions failures "egregious and continued." It also linked the missed transactions to suspected Chinese money-laundering networks and to illicit finance around the southern US border.
That is a serious set of claims against one of the largest banks in the world. In a cleaner era of financial reporting, a headline like this would ripple straight through risk assets. Instead, it barely registered anywhere.
Bitcoin was trading near $83,117 as the news crossed, up a rounding-error 0.1% on the day. Ethereum sat near $2,504, down less than 1%. Neither chart shows a flinch tied to this story.
That non-reaction is itself the story. A decade ago, a scandal at a systemic bank was a market event by default. Now the asset class built partly as an answer to opaque banking plumbing treated it as background noise.
There is a quiet irony here. A penalty for failing to track money moving through an opaque system arrived while crypto, the transparent-ledger alternative, kept trading as if nothing happened. We are not pretending this fine is a crypto catalyst. It is not. But it is a useful marker of how far these two worlds have drifted apart.
Why a legacy-bank penalty skips crypto plumbing
The transmission mechanism here is the interesting part, because there barely is one. A fine on a traditional bank hits that bank's capital and its compliance costs. It does not drain liquidity from crypto exchanges, change dollar funding, or move the rates that actually steer risk appetite.
So the chain that usually matters, driver to macro to liquidity to BTC, breaks at the first link. There is no macro shock. There is no liquidity withdrawal. There is nothing for Bitcoin or Ethereum to price.
What this fine does signal is direction of travel. Regulators are leaning harder on anti-money-laundering, or AML, which is the duty to flag suspicious flows, and on sanctions compliance. That pressure sits on legacy finance first, where the $5 billion in missed transactions actually moved.
Here is the structural read, stated as our analysis, not fact. Every time a large bank is penalised for failing to police opaque flows, the case for transparent, auditable ledgers gets quietly stronger. A public chain does not "miss" transactions. They are all there, permanently, for anyone to inspect.
That is a slow, long-horizon tailwind, not a trade. It will not show up on today's candle. It shows up across cycles, in which rails institutions choose to trust.
For now the honest takeaway is narrow. This is a traditional-finance story with a traditional-finance price, and the crypto market has correctly treated it as someone else's problem.
Reading the non-reaction across BTC and alts
Start with what did not happen, because that is the signal. There was no liquidity cascade from this fine. BTC did not lead a move, so ETH and alts had nothing to follow.
Bitcoin held near $83,117, flat on the day and up a sliver in the last hour. That is a market ignoring a headline, not absorbing a shock. When price refuses to react to scary-sounding news, it usually means the news never touched the order book in the first place.
Ethereum tells the same story from the softer side. It traded near $2,504, down under 1% over 24 hours. That mild weakness is ordinary chop against BTC, not a reaction to a bank penalty. Nothing in the alt complex is pricing contagion from Bank of America.
The cleaner way to frame it: crypto has largely decoupled from this flavour of traditional-finance headline. A fine, even a billion-dollar one, is a corporate event for one bank. It is not a systemic liquidity event like a failure or a credit freeze would be.
That distinction matters for how you weight it. A bank collapse pulls dollar liquidity and drags everything. A bank fine is a line item. Markets know the difference, and today they priced it as such.
So the impact read is neutral by construction. This story, on its own facts, gives neither bulls nor bears fresh fuel in crypto. The real drivers for BTC and ETH sit elsewhere on the chart.
When a bank scandal would actually hit crypto
The thing to watch is not this fine. It is whether this fine is a one-off or the opening of a wider enforcement wave across major banks.
A single penalty is noise for crypto. A pattern is different. If enforcement broadens into funding stress, frozen credit lines, or a systemic bank in real trouble, that becomes a liquidity story, and liquidity stories do reach Bitcoin fast.
So the confirmation we would actually care about is macro, not legal. Watch dollar funding conditions and any sign that bank balance-sheet strain is tightening credit. Those are the channels through which traditional finance stress historically leaks into risk assets.
The invalidation of any "this matters for crypto" thesis is simply the chart itself. As long as BTC keeps trading on its own structure near $83,000 and ignores these headlines, the decoupling thesis holds.
There is also the slower thread to monitor. If regulators keep punishing opaque legacy plumbing, the long-term case for transparent ledgers strengthens. That is a narrative to track across quarters, not a level to trade this week.
One honest caveat. We have no single confirmed same-day catalyst driving crypto right now, so attributing any small move to this fine would be a mistake. The responsible position is to watch the bank-sector follow-through and let Bitcoin's own levels, not this headline, dictate the next real move.
What this fine means for Bitcoin positioning now
The ParadiseTeam view is direct: this fine changes nothing on the Bitcoin chart, so trade the structure, not the headline. BTC was near $83,117 as the news crossed, and the levels that matter are the ones that already mattered.
On the current market lens, the short-term bias stays constructive. The team is watching the $81,500 support, with $81,000 beneath it, as the zone that must hold for the bullish structure to stay intact. A dip toward $81,500 reads as a healthy correction, not a reversal, and this bank fine does not alter that.
To the upside, the line in the sand is the previous high at $83,400. Reclaiming and holding above it keeps the path toward the $90,000 short-term target open. Failing there just means more range, again unrelated to any bank headline.
The smart-money versus retail read sits entirely in that price structure, not in this story. The team continues to see accumulation absorbing fearful retail selling, with whales net buyers and open interest making lower lows as retail closes longs. That is the real tell, and it is doing its own thing regardless of Treasury press releases.
So the discipline here is to not manufacture a trade out of unrelated news. This is a traditional-finance event with a traditional-finance price. Let the $81,500 support and the $83,400 reclaim decide the next move, and treat the bank fine as context, not a signal.
